• D) - Cholecystokinin

questions.question: Explain the functioning of Benedict Roth Respirometer.
questions.solution_html:
• Diagram – (1mark)
  • The apparatus consists of a bell spirometer, a kymograph drum, timer, mouthpiece and its
  • attachments. The bell spirometer is a hollow double walled cylindrical vessel. The space
  • between the two walls contain water. A hollow cylindrical bell fits inverted between the
  • double walled vessel. A can containing soda lime is placed inside the double walled vessel.
  • Kymograph drum is a revolving drum with a kymograph sheet fixed on it. It is attached to
  • inverted vessel with the help of a pulley on one side and the other end has a pen attached to
  • drum. A timer is attached to kymograph drum such that when timer starts, drum starts
  • revolving at a speed in which it completes one rotation in one minute. The thermometer
  • attached to the apparatus measures the room temperature. The mouth piece has two tubes, one
  • supplies oxygen for inspiration and other attached to can containing soda lime through which
  • expired air passes. The tubes are regulated by valves such that it functions in one way
  • direction.
  • The subject is asked to sit or lie down quietly for the test. The spirometer is filled with
  • oxygen. The mouthpiece is inserted to the mouth of the subject and nose is clipped. The
  • subject is asked to breathe slowly through the mouth. When breathing is regular, connect him
  • to apparatus by switching on oxygen supply. Then switch on the timer. As the subject
  • breathes, spirometer bell moves up and down. As the movement of spirometer progresses, the
  • graph is recorded on the drum. Continue recording for 8-20 minutes. From the graph the
  • metabolic rate can be determined by calculation method. ( (4 marks))
questions.final_answer: metabolic rate can be determined by calculation method.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Discuss the role of fibre in preventing colon cancer.
questions.solution_html:
•  The fibre dilutes bile acids or binds to it thereby preventing its role in mutation
  • or cell proliferation. Fermentation of dietary fibre results in production of short
  • chain fatty acids lowering the intestinal pH. This inhibits conversion of primary
  • bile acids to secondary bile acids.
  •  The secondary bile acids are believed to promote mutation in intestine. At low
  • pH the solubility of free bile acids is reduced, diminishing their availability for
  • carcinogenic activity. Fermentation of dietary fibre results in production of
  • butyrate which has been shown to be antineoplastic.
  •  Dietary fibre exerts its beneficial effect by speeding the passage of faeces
  • through the large intestine so that carcinogens are in contact with the intestinal
  • wall for much shorter period of time. Additionally the bulk and water of the
  • faeces may dilute the carcinogen to a nontoxic level.
  •  Dietary fibre also influences the colonic microbial metabolism, influences
  • fermentation in the colon and the production and distribution of short chain
  • fatty acids in the colon. It modifies pH, increases the faecal nitrogen and
  • influences mutagens and faecal enzymes in the colon.
  •  Fructo Oligo Saccharides have both complementary and overlapping
  • mechanism of action, including the induction of detoxification enzymes
  • inhibition of nitrosamine formation, provision of substrate for formation of
  • antineoplastic agents, dilution and binding of carcinogens in the digestive tract
  • alteration of hormone metabolism and antioxidant effects. It appears extremely
  • unlikely that any one substance is responsible for all the associations seen.
  • ( (1 mark) for each point)

questions.question: Discuss the clinical features of pellagra
questions.solution_html:
• The typical clinical features are loss of weight and increased debility. The deficiency
  • disease is Pellagra, called as the disease of 3 Ds: Dermatitis, Diarrhoea and Dementia
  • leading to death, the fourth D. ((2 Marks))
  •  Dermal lesions - photo sensitive rash and are seen in exposed surface of body and are
  • hyper pigmented. The lesions are percipated on exposure to sunlight, fire and radiant
  • heat. On neck it is called Casal’s Necklace.((1 Mark))
  •  Gastrointestinal changes: Mucous membrane is inflamed resulting in severe glossitis
  • stomatitis, oesophagitis and gastritis and enteritis. The inflammation can produce
  • bloody diarrhoea.((1 Mark))
  •  Neurological manifestation: Insomnia, hallucination, delirium etc develops. The
  • peripheral nerve may be affected with paraesthesia and decreased nerve conduction
  • incoordination and tremors, Spastic paraplegiaand exaggerated deep tendon reflexes
  • are observed.((1Mark))

questions.question: Explain the process of absorption and metabolism of phosphorus Part D Essay
questions.solution_html:
•  Inorganic phosphorus is readily absorbed, while organic phosphorus may require
  • enzymatic breakdownfor efficient absorption. ((1 mark))
  •  The majority of phosphorus absorption takes place particularly in the duodenum. A
  • significant portion of phosphorus is absorbed through passive diffusion. Some
  • phosphorus absorption also involves active transport.((1 mark))
  •  Hormones like parathyroid hormone (PTH) and vitamin D play a crucial role in
  • regulating the absorption and utilization of phosphorus. ((1 mark))
  •  In healthy people the rate at which phosphorus absorption and excretion is equal
  • maintaining total body phosphorus at a steady level. ((1 mark))
  •  Approximately 90 per cent of ingested phosphorus is excreted through urine, with the
  • remaining 10 per cent lost directly from the gastrointestinal tract without being
  • absorbed. If plasma phosphorus levels decline, reabsorption by the kidneys increases
  • to compensate and if plasma phosphorus levels rise too high, no phosphorus is
  • reabsorbed in the kidneys.((1 mark))
  • Essay

questions.question: Explain the digestion, absorption and transport of carbohydrates.
questions.solution_html:
•  Digestion of polysaccharides begins in the mouth with salivary amylase or
  • ptyalin or α-amylase released during the process of chewing.
  •  The amylase is synthesized in the serous cells of the salivary glands. Amylase
  • breaks starches into maltose and polysaccharides. Amylase is sensitive to pH
  • and thus is inhibited in the acidic environment of the stomach.
  •  Pancreatic amylase is released from acinar cells into the small intestine in
  • concert with other enzymes under the stimulus of secretin and cholecystokinin
  • and continues the process of carbohydrate digestion.
  •  Starch is digested in the small intestine to simple components.
  • Oligosaccharides and disaccharides are digested by specific enzymes in the
  • microvillus membrane (brush border). These enzymes include maltase that
  • break down maltose to two glucose molecules, sucrase which digests sucrose to
  • fructose and glucose and lactase helps to digest lactose to galactose and
  • glucose.
  •  Carbohydrates not digested in the small intestine pass into the large intestine
  • where they are digested by colonic bacteria. This results in the release of short
  • chain fatty acids like propionate, butyrate and acetate along with methane.
  •  The short chain fatty acids provide vital nutrition to colonocytes, but excess
  • volumes induce diarrhea and abdominal cramping. ( (7 marks))
  • Absorption and Transport
  •  Carbohydrates are absorbed into the blood stream as glucose, galactose and
  • fructose. The simple sugars enter portal circulation via the capillaries of
  • intestinal villi and are transported to the liver. The fructose and galactose are
  • converted to glycogen for storage.
  •  Glucose and Na+ share the same transport system. The concentration of Na+ is
  • higher in the intestinal lumen compared to mucosal cells. Na+ moves into the
  • cells along its concentration gradient and simultaneously glucose is transported
  • into the intestinal cells. This is mediated by the same carrier system. This
  • energy is indirectly supplied by ATP
  •  The absorption of glucose is affected by the amount of sodium (Na) ions in the
  • intestinal lumen. A high Na+ concentration facilitates glucose influx into the
  • intestinal mucosal cell, whereas a low Na+ concentration inhibits influx. ( 3
  • marks)

questions.question: Explain folate deficiency, causes, clinical features and its effect on foetal development
questions.solution_html:
• Causes
  •  Poor dietary intake: due to poor intake of milk, fruits and vegetables.
  •  Low absorption: due to vitamin C deficiency, celiac disease,tropical sprue, impaired
  • absorption in pregnancy. Vitamin B12 deficiency can also result in folate deficiency.
  •  Increased losses: it occur in haemodialysis
  •  Increased requirement: increased requirement due to growth and pregnancy.
  •  Infestation and infection: malarial infection and parasitic infestation.
  •  Drugs: anticonvulsant drugs and oral contraceptives may impair folate absorption.
  •  Chronic alcoholism also causes deficiency.
  • ((3 Marks))
  • Megaloblastic Anaemia
  • Both vitamin B12 and folate are essential for DNA synthesis and deficiency of either or
  • both causes a failure of DNA synthesis and disordered cell proliferation. Haemopoesis is
  • particularly susceptible and division of cells is delayed and eventually halted.
  • Morphological changes appear in the bone marrow leads to increase in RBC size.
  • ((1 Mark))
  • Clinical features
  • Symptoms like weakness, tiredness, dyspnoea, sore tongue, diarrhoea, irritability and
  • forgetfulness, anorexia, headache and palpitation are seen. There is weight loss. Glossitis
  • is less common. Neurological problems are very rare. ((2 Marks))
  • Folate deficiency during pregnancy – Folic acid is needed for the synthesis of essential
  • components of DNA and RNA which increases rapidly during growth, thereby
  • increasing the requirements.
  • There is decrease in folate absorption and an increase in urinary excretion during
  • pregnancy. Folate deficiency causes damage to the developing foetus. It causes neural
  • tube defectssuch as Spina bifidaandAnencephaly.Because the neural tube closes by 28
  • days of gestation, supplementation with folic acid prior to conception is useful.
  • ((4 Marks))

questions.question: Describe the absorption, transport, storage, and metabolism of iron in the human body
questions.solution_html:
• body
  • Absorption - Iron is absorbed in the duodenum and upper part of jejunum where it can
  • exist in two forms - haeme and non-haeme iron. Haeme iron, is more easily absorbed than
  • non-haeme iron. Iron in food can be in the ferric or ferrous form. At the acidic pH of the
  • stomach, ferric iron can be converted to the more soluble ferrous form.Heme iron is
  • absorbed directly into the intestinal cells (enterocytes). Non-heme iron is converted to
  • ferrous iron by duodenal cytochrome b.((4 Marks))
  • Transport- Once inside the enterocyte, iron can be stored as ferritin and is transported
  • across the basolateral membrane into the bloodstream via ferroportin. In the
  • bloodstream, iron is bound to transferrin. A significant portion of iron is transported to
  • the bone marrow. Iron is also transported to liver and spleen. ((2 Marks))
  • Storage - Iron is stored in cells, primarily in the liver and spleen, as ferritin. When ferritin
  • storage capacity is exceeded, iron can also be stored as hemosiderin, a more insoluble
  • form. ((2 Marks))
  • Metabolism - When red blood cells are broken down, the iron is released and can be
  • recycled for erythropoiesis or stored. Between 200 and 1500 mg of iron is stored in the
  • body as ferritin and hemosiderin; 30% is in the liver, 30% is in the bone marrow, and the
  • rest is in the spleen and muscles. Iron is lost from the body only through bleeding and in
  • very small amounts through defecation, sweat, and the normal exfoliation of hair and
  • skin. Daily iron loss is approximately 1 mg for men and slightly less for non-menstruating
  • women. The loss of iron accompanying menstruation averages approximately 0.5 mg/day.
  • ((2 Marks))

questions.question: Explain the functioning of Benedict Roth Respirometer.
questions.solution_html:
• Diagram – (1mark)
  • The apparatus consists of a bell spirometer, a kymograph drum, timer, mouthpiece and its
  • attachments. The bell spirometer is a hollow double walled cylindrical vessel. The space
  • between the two walls contain water. A hollow cylindrical bell fits inverted between the
  • double walled vessel. A can containing soda lime is placed inside the double walled vessel.
  • Kymograph drum is a revolving drum with a kymograph sheet fixed on it. It is attached to
  • inverted vessel with the help of a pulley on one side and the other end has a pen attached to
  • drum. A timer is attached to kymograph drum such that when timer starts, drum starts
  • revolving at a speed in which it completes one rotation in one minute. The thermometer
  • attached to the apparatus measures the room temperature. The mouth piece has two tubes, one
  • supplies oxygen for inspiration and other attached to can containing soda lime through which
  • expired air passes. The tubes are regulated by valves such that it functions in one way
  • direction.
  • The subject is asked to sit or lie down quietly for the test. The spirometer is filled with
  • oxygen. The mouthpiece is inserted to the mouth of the subject and nose is clipped. The
  • subject is asked to breathe slowly through the mouth. When breathing is regular, connect him
  • to apparatus by switching on oxygen supply. Then switch on the timer. As the subject
  • breathes, spirometer bell moves up and down. As the movement of spirometer progresses, the
  • graph is recorded on the drum. Continue recording for 8-20 minutes. From the graph the
  • metabolic rate can be determined by calculation method. ( (4 marks))
questions.final_answer: metabolic rate can be determined by calculation method.

questions.question: Discuss the role of fibre in preventing colon cancer.
questions.solution_html:
•  The fibre dilutes bile acids or binds to it thereby preventing its role in mutation
  • or cell proliferation. Fermentation of dietary fibre results in production of short
  • chain fatty acids lowering the intestinal pH. This inhibits conversion of primary
  • bile acids to secondary bile acids.
  •  The secondary bile acids are believed to promote mutation in intestine. At low
  • pH the solubility of free bile acids is reduced, diminishing their availability for
  • carcinogenic activity. Fermentation of dietary fibre results in production of
  • butyrate which has been shown to be antineoplastic.
  •  Dietary fibre exerts its beneficial effect by speeding the passage of faeces
  • through the large intestine so that carcinogens are in contact with the intestinal
  • wall for much shorter period of time. Additionally the bulk and water of the
  • faeces may dilute the carcinogen to a nontoxic level.
  •  Dietary fibre also influences the colonic microbial metabolism, influences
  • fermentation in the colon and the production and distribution of short chain
  • fatty acids in the colon. It modifies pH, increases the faecal nitrogen and
  • influences mutagens and faecal enzymes in the colon.
  •  Fructo Oligo Saccharides have both complementary and overlapping
  • mechanism of action, including the induction of detoxification enzymes
  • inhibition of nitrosamine formation, provision of substrate for formation of
  • antineoplastic agents, dilution and binding of carcinogens in the digestive tract
  • alteration of hormone metabolism and antioxidant effects. It appears extremely
  • unlikely that any one substance is responsible for all the associations seen.
  • ( (1 mark) for each point)

questions.question: Explain the digestion, absorption and transport of carbohydrates.
questions.solution_html:
•  Digestion of polysaccharides begins in the mouth with salivary amylase or
  • ptyalin or α-amylase released during the process of chewing.
  •  The amylase is synthesized in the serous cells of the salivary glands. Amylase
  • breaks starches into maltose and polysaccharides. Amylase is sensitive to pH
  • and thus is inhibited in the acidic environment of the stomach.
  •  Pancreatic amylase is released from acinar cells into the small intestine in
  • concert with other enzymes under the stimulus of secretin and cholecystokinin
  • and continues the process of carbohydrate digestion.
  •  Starch is digested in the small intestine to simple components.
  • Oligosaccharides and disaccharides are digested by specific enzymes in the
  • microvillus membrane (brush border). These enzymes include maltase that
  • break down maltose to two glucose molecules, sucrase which digests sucrose to
  • fructose and glucose and lactase helps to digest lactose to galactose and
  • glucose.
  •  Carbohydrates not digested in the small intestine pass into the large intestine
  • where they are digested by colonic bacteria. This results in the release of short
  • chain fatty acids like propionate, butyrate and acetate along with methane.
  •  The short chain fatty acids provide vital nutrition to colonocytes, but excess
  • volumes induce diarrhea and abdominal cramping. ( (7 marks))
  • Absorption and Transport
  •  Carbohydrates are absorbed into the blood stream as glucose, galactose and
  • fructose. The simple sugars enter portal circulation via the capillaries of
  • intestinal villi and are transported to the liver. The fructose and galactose are
  • converted to glycogen for storage.
  •  Glucose and Na+ share the same transport system. The concentration of Na+ is
  • higher in the intestinal lumen compared to mucosal cells. Na+ moves into the
  • cells along its concentration gradient and simultaneously glucose is transported
  • into the intestinal cells. This is mediated by the same carrier system. This
  • energy is indirectly supplied by ATP
  •  The absorption of glucose is affected by the amount of sodium (Na) ions in the
  • intestinal lumen. A high Na+ concentration facilitates glucose influx into the
  • intestinal mucosal cell, whereas a low Na+ concentration inhibits influx. ( 3
  • marks)

questions.question: Explain folate deficiency, causes, clinical features and its effect on foetal development

  •  Low absorption: due to vitamin C deficiency, celiac disease,tropical sprue, impaired
  • absorption in pregnancy. Vitamin B12 deficiency can also result in folate deficiency.
  •  Increased losses: it occur in haemodialysis
  •  Increased requirement: increased requirement due to growth and pregnancy.
  •  Infestation and infection: malarial infection and parasitic infestation.
  •  Drugs: anticonvulsant drugs and oral contraceptives may impair folate absorption.
  •  Chronic alcoholism also causes deficiency.
  • ((3 Marks))
  • Megaloblastic Anaemia
  • Both vitamin B12 and folate are essential for DNA synthesis and deficiency of either or
  • both causes a failure of DNA synthesis and disordered cell proliferation. Haemopoesis is
  • particularly susceptible and division of cells is delayed and eventually halted.
  • Morphological changes appear in the bone marrow leads to increase in RBC size.

  • Symptoms like weakness, tiredness, dyspnoea, sore tongue, diarrhoea, irritability and
  • forgetfulness, anorexia, headache and palpitation are seen. There is weight loss. Glossitis
  • is less common. Neurological problems are very rare. ((2 Marks))
  • Folate deficiency during pregnancy – Folic acid is needed for the synthesis of essential
  • components of DNA and RNA which increases rapidly during growth, thereby
  • increasing the requirements.
  • There is decrease in folate absorption and an increase in urinary excretion during
  • pregnancy. Folate deficiency causes damage to the developing foetus. It causes neural
  • tube defectssuch as Spina bifidaandAnencephaly.Because the neural tube closes by 28
  • days of gestation, supplementation with folic acid prior to conception is useful.
  • ((4 Marks))

questions.question: Describe the absorption, transport, storage, and metabolism of iron in the human body
questions.solution_html:
• body
  • Absorption - Iron is absorbed in the duodenum and upper part of jejunum where it can
  • exist in two forms - haeme and non-haeme iron. Haeme iron, is more easily absorbed than
  • non-haeme iron. Iron in food can be in the ferric or ferrous form. At the acidic pH of the
  • stomach, ferric iron can be converted to the more soluble ferrous form.Heme iron is
  • absorbed directly into the intestinal cells (enterocytes). Non-heme iron is converted to
  • ferrous iron by duodenal cytochrome b.((4 Marks))
  • Transport- Once inside the enterocyte, iron can be stored as ferritin and is transported
  • across the basolateral membrane into the bloodstream via ferroportin. In the
  • bloodstream, iron is bound to transferrin. A significant portion of iron is transported to
  • the bone marrow. Iron is also transported to liver and spleen. ((2 Marks))
  • Storage - Iron is stored in cells, primarily in the liver and spleen, as ferritin. When ferritin
  • storage capacity is exceeded, iron can also be stored as hemosiderin, a more insoluble
  • form. ((2 Marks))
  • Metabolism - When red blood cells are broken down, the iron is released and can be
  • recycled for erythropoiesis or stored. Between 200 and 1500 mg of iron is stored in the
  • body as ferritin and hemosiderin; 30% is in the liver, 30% is in the bone marrow, and the
  • rest is in the spleen and muscles. Iron is lost from the body only through bleeding and in
  • very small amounts through defecation, sweat, and the normal exfoliation of hair and
  • skin. Daily iron loss is approximately 1 mg for men and slightly less for non-menstruating
  • women. The loss of iron accompanying menstruation averages approximately 0.5 mg/day.
  • ((2 Marks))
